newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy 1996 PSBR seen at some 140 trln lire - Il Sole.
newsitem.headline: Italy 1996 PSBR seen at some 140 trln lire - Il Sole.

text.p: Italy's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) for 1996 will overshoot government targets and come in at around 140 trillion lire ($93 billion), financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said on Sunday.

The government's target for this year's deficit has been revised upwards several times with the last official figure set in October at 123 trillion, but government officials have since indicated a deficit of some 130 trillion lire was more likely.
Il Sole said provisional estimates were for a November PSBR of around 20 trillion lire, making a cumulative total for the first 11 months of around 136 trillion lire.
It said December's deficit would be around four trillion.

Several economists have warned that the government's draft budget, designed to lop 62.5 trillion lire off next year's projected deficit, might not be enough to bring Italy's deficit/GDP ratio down to the 3.0 percent parameter for 1999 entry into European economic and monetary union.

Banca Commerciale Italiana (BCI) analysts, forecasting a 1996 PSBR of 137 trillion lire, said last week Italy might need an extra 25 trillion lire "mini-budget" early in 1997 to reach the 3.0 percent Maastricht goal.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday he was counting on Italy meeting deficit conditions in 1997 for membership of Europe's planned single currency after telling a newspaper that the country would miss the target.
Prodi issued a statement on the sensitive issue after an interview in Friday's International Herald Tribune (IHT).
It had quoted him as saying the ratio between the budget deficit and Gross Domestic Product in 1997 would be 3.3 percent.

Prodi said in the statement that he had cited 3.3 percent "out of prudence and honesty" because it was the estimate made by the European Commission and because Italy's 1997 budget had not yet been approved by both houses of parliament.
"I stuck to the figures which readers of the newspaper know better," Prodi said.
"Naturally, with approval of the budget by both houses of parliament, the government is counting on meeting the target (of 3.0 percent) contained in the budget itself," Prodi said.
The 62.5 trillion lire budget for 1997, one of the toughest in years, is currently making its way through parliament and must be approved by the end of the year.

"In all honesty we will get to 3.3 percent, rather than an exact three percent, meaning we will be in the range," Prodi had told the IHT. "And then we will examine with our European colleagues what we need to do," he said.
He added that in order to meet the Maastricht goal he was prepared "to take extraordinary and supplementary steps if that is deemed necessary."
To avoid having to introduce a supplementary budget in the spring Italy would need a growth rate of two percent in 1997, the IHT quoted Prodi as saying.
But many economists and even the authoritative Bank of Italy have forecast 1997 GDP growth of little over one percent after a targeted 0.8 percent rate for this year.

However, an optimistic deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni said in Sunday's Corriere della Sera, "No one has spoken of an extra budget, nothing of the kind. The worst is behind us and I feel able to say we're at the end of the tunnel."
